newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW - Foreign banks slug it out in Mexico.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Foreign banks slug it out in Mexico.

text.p: Two-and-a-half-years after the crushing peso crash, Mexico's banking sector is again a tough market for foreign banks slugging it out for business, the head of Dresdner Bank in Mexico said.
"The competition in Mexico is brutal," said Luis Nino de Rivera, director general in Mexico for Dresdner, one of Germany's largest banks.
There are about 106 foreign banks represented in Mexico, and a good portion of them offer a full-range of services.

"Each time some business appears so do all the banks, and moreover, there are international brokerage houses and investment banks who are also here. The competition is very intense," he said in an interview.

"A bond, a syndicated loan, the sale or purchase of a company, an infrastructure privatization, whatever you want, there is a scrap to lead them, with lots of very tough competitors," he said in the interview conducted Thursday.
Still, the recovery in Mexico -- shown in various economic statistics -- offers some good opportunities.

He said that in the two-and-a-half years since the economic crisis, Mexico has proven that its recovery is underway, although he added that growth still needs to become sustainable. Real wage growth could also be better, he noted.
He said the July 6 mid-term elections -- generally considered fair and clean -- had a positive effect on perceptions of Mexico abroad.
"Among the emerging markets Mexico has become an attractive investment," he added.
Dresdner offers a number of banking services, with one of the latest being asset management through five new mututal funds operating on the Mexican stock exchange through a subsidiary.
The funds are aimed at individuals and groups that need professional fund management.
"There are a lot of companies with liquidity that need professional consulting and administration. We believe there is an economy big enough to attract resources for those funds," he said.
"We are trying to make them grow at least to 1.0 billion pesos for each fund," he said. "I would calculate that this could take this year and the coming year."
Dresdner is the third foreign bank to set up its own mutual funds in Mexico.
Many Mexican banks also run their own mutual funds, which Nino de Rivera called, "very good and very competitive."
Three of Dresdner's funds are fixed income and the other two equity funds.
"All are instruments in pesos in the Mexican market, with shares listed on the Mexican stock exchange or debt instruments of the government, government entities or private companies," he said.
Dresdner has also participated in a number of bond placements for the Mexican government, helping to build a yield curve in marks.
"We have found an interesting demand in Germany for this paper," he said, noting that yields are tight on German debt instruments.
"A (Mexican) instrument that can pay investors seven or eight percent in marks becomes attractive against the three or four percent that instruments pay there," he said.
Since late 1995, the United Mexican States, the formal name for the federal government, has floated five mark denominated bonds.
((--Mexico City newsroom +525 728 9559))
